transcript.text: theres a funny smell from my oven when its on

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. An oven smell can mean anything from harmless baked-on spills to an electrical connection overheating, and from here I can't tell which. So please don't use it again until a qualified engineer has checked it, and switch it off at the cooker isolator switch (the big switch on the wall nearby) or at the consumer unit. 1. Food, fat or oven-cleaner residue burning off on the oven floor, the walls or a heating element. This usually smells of burnt food or smoky grease and is strongest when you open the door.
2. The mains terminal block at the back, where the supply cable connects, overheating because of a loose or poor connection. This tends to smell of hot plastic, a bit fishy or "electrical", and often seems to come from the back of the cooker rather than the cavity.
3. A heating element starting to fail. That can overheat the connection it's wired to and give a similar electrical smell. These checks are safe with the oven isolated and fully cooled down. 1. Open the door and look inside with a torch. Check the floor, the walls, the grill area and the fan cover for spills or a heavy build-up of grease, and any leftover cleaner. Lots of residue points towards cause 1.
2. Note any blistering, splits or bright marks, which suggest a failing element.
3. If you can see the back of the cooker without pulling it out, look for scorching or discolouration around where the cable goes in. Don't unscrew any covers. Any sign of heat damage there points strongly at the terminal block or supply connection, and that is fixed mains wiring, so it's an engineer job. What kind of smell is it, and where does it seem to come from? That's the quickest way to tell these apart.

its more like hot plastic or electrical burning, and it seems to come from behind or underneath, not inside the oven. the cooker switch on the wall looks a bit brown at one corner and felt warm, the kitchen lights flickered once, and I heard a crackle from the back once. I can't pull the cooker out to look, its too heavy

⚠ Stop using this appliance
That combination points firmly at an overheating electrical connection in the cooker's supply, not anything inside the oven. 1. The wall cooker switch itself, or the cable terminals behind it. Browning and warmth on the switch plate is direct evidence of heat there.
2. The mains terminal block on the back of the cooker, where the supply cable connects. A crackle from the back fits this well, and a bad connection at one end often damages the other. A failing heating element can occasionally overheat its own connection too, but that wouldn't explain the warm wall switch, so it's a distant third. This isn't something to check yourself. It's fixed mains wiring and an active fire risk, so please don't use the cooker again until it has been checked. 1. Don't touch or operate the discoloured wall switch. Turn off the cooker's circuit breaker at the consumer unit (fuse box) instead. It's usually labelled "cooker" or "oven".
2. If the smell carries on, or you see smoke or the switch plate gets hotter even with the breaker off, get everyone out and call 999.
3. Book a qualified electrician (NICEIC or NAPIT registered) rather than an appliance engineer first. They can inspect and replace the cooker switch, check the cable and circuit, and pull the cooker out safely to look at its terminal block, so you don't need to move it yourself. The good news is that a burnt cooker switch or terminal block is usually a modest, routine repair, and the cooker itself is often fine afterwards. The electrician will tell you if the damage reaches the cooker's own terminal block or an element.
